title: How to Get Rid of Alcohol Breath: What Works and What Doesn't
excerpt: Why alcohol breath comes from your lungs, not just your mouth, what actually helps the morning after, why you can smell like alcohol the next day, and when a breath smell needs a doctor.
metaDescription: How to get rid of alcohol breath: why mints don't fully work, what actually helps, why you smell like alcohol the next day, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how to get rid of alcohol breath
content:
**The honest answer first:** you can't fully get rid of alcohol breath until your body has finished processing the alcohol. The smell isn't only coming from your mouth. Some alcohol travels from your blood into your lungs and leaves with every breath you exhale, and some leaves through your skin and sweat. Mints, gum, and mouthwash can cover the part that comes from your mouth, but nothing you chew or gargle can reach your lungs. What actually works is a mix of time, food, water, cleaning your mouth properly, and a shower and fresh clothes. This guide explains where the smell comes from, which fixes help and which don't, why you can still smell like alcohol the next morning, and when a strange breath smell deserves a doctor.

**The quick plan for the morning after:**

1. Brush your teeth *and* your tongue, then floss.
2. Drink a big glass of water, and keep sipping through the morning.
3. Eat a real breakfast. Food gets saliva flowing and gives your mouth something other than stale alcohol to smell of.
4. Shower, and put on clean clothes. Last night's shirt holds the smell.
5. Use mints, gum, or a strong-flavored food as a cover for the mouth part.
6. Accept that the lung part only fades with time. If you still smell strongly of alcohol, there is a good chance you still have alcohol in your blood, so don't drive.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research about how the body handles alcohol. **See a doctor if** your breath smells of alcohol or nail-polish remover when you haven't been drinking, your breath smells fruity or sweet and you also feel very thirsty, are peeing a lot, or are vomiting, or you notice confusion, fast breathing, or stomach pain along with an unusual breath smell. These can be signs of a serious problem such as diabetic ketoacidosis. If someone who has been drinking is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, has bluish or pale skin, or is vomiting while drowsy, call 911. That is an emergency, not a breath problem.

## Why Your Breath Smells Like Alcohol: It Starts in Your Lungs

Most bad breath comes from the mouth: bacteria on the tongue and between the teeth break down food and release smelly sulfur compounds. Alcohol breath is different, and that difference is why the usual fixes fall short.

When you drink, alcohol is absorbed through your stomach and small intestine into your bloodstream. Your blood then passes through your lungs, where it sits right next to tiny air sacs. Because alcohol evaporates easily, a small amount of it moves out of the blood and into the air in those sacs. When you breathe out, that air carries the alcohol with it. This is the same principle a breathalyzer relies on: the amount of alcohol in your breath tracks the amount in your blood.

Your liver does most of the work of clearing alcohol. It breaks the large majority down, first into a compound called acetaldehyde and then into acetic acid (the main acid in vinegar), and finally into carbon dioxide and water. Only a small share leaves your body unchanged, through your breath, urine, and sweat. But that small share is enough for people around you to notice.

So alcohol breath has several layers:

- **Alcohol from your lungs.** This is the main source, and it lasts as long as alcohol is in your blood.
- **Leftover drink in your mouth.** Traces of beer, wine, or spirits on your teeth, tongue, and gums. This part fades fast and is easy to clean.
- **The flavor compounds in the drink itself.** Alcohol on its own has only a faint smell. Much of the classic "boozy" odor comes from what drinkers call congeners and flavorings: hops and grain in beer, the compounds in red wine, the botanicals in gin. Some of these linger on the breath too.
- **By-products of breaking alcohol down.** As your body processes alcohol, by-products can add a stale, slightly sour note to your breath and skin.
- **A dry mouth.** Alcohol makes you pee more and reduces saliva. Saliva normally washes away bacteria, so a dry mouth smells worse on its own, which piles on top of everything else. Our guide to [dry mouth after drinking](/never-hungover/dry-mouth-after-drinking) explains this part in more detail.

## Why Mints, Gum, and Mouthwash Don't Fully Work

Since much of the smell comes from your lungs, anything that works only in your mouth can only cover the top layer. That doesn't make these products useless. It just sets realistic expectations.

- **Mints and gum** cover the smell with a stronger one for a few minutes. Sugar-free gum also gets saliva flowing, which genuinely helps with dry-mouth odor. But the alcohol coming from your lungs keeps arriving with every breath, so the cover wears off quickly.
- **Mouthwash** kills bacteria and freshens the mouth, which helps with the dry-mouth layer. Be aware that many mouthwashes contain alcohol themselves. Using one right before you talk to someone can make you smell *more* like alcohol for a little while, not less. An alcohol-free mouthwash is a better choice here.
- **Strong flavors** like coffee, garlic, or onion can cover alcohol breath, but they swap one smell for another and don't remove anything.

The key idea: covering a smell is not the same as clearing alcohol. Mints can make you smell fresher to a coworker standing nearby, but they do nothing to lower your blood alcohol level or a breathalyzer reading.

## How to Get Rid of Alcohol Breath: What Actually Helps

Here are the steps that make a real difference, in rough order of how much they help.

### 1. Give it time

This is the only thing that removes the lung part of the smell. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, often quoted as about one standard drink per hour, though it varies a lot between people. There's no way to make your liver work dramatically faster. Coffee, cold showers, exercise, and "detox" drinks don't change that rate in any meaningful way. Our guide to [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up) walks through the math for different numbers of drinks.

### 2. Clean your whole mouth, including your tongue

Brush your teeth for a full two minutes, then brush or scrape your tongue. The back of the tongue holds a lot of the bacteria that cause bad breath, and it's the spot most people skip. Floss to remove anything trapped between teeth. This won't touch the lung smell, but it removes the mouth layer completely.

### 3. Drink water, and keep drinking it

Water helps in two ways. It rinses your mouth and gets saliva flowing again, and it helps you recover from the fluid you lost by peeing more while drinking. It won't flush alcohol out of your blood faster in any meaningful way, but a hydrated mouth simply smells better. Our article on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers how much fluid you actually lose.

### 4. Eat a proper breakfast

Eating does several useful things at once. Chewing gets saliva going. Food gives your mouth a different, stronger smell to work with. And if you still have alcohol in your stomach, food can slow how quickly the rest is absorbed. Foods that need a lot of chewing, like toast, apples, or crunchy vegetables, are especially good at stimulating saliva. Eggs are a popular choice and a decent one, as we explain in our piece on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).

### 5. Shower and change your clothes

This step is underrated. Alcohol and its by-products leave your body through your skin and sweat, too. Devices that monitor drinking through the skin, like the ankle bracelets some courts use, work on exactly this principle. If you slept in last night's clothes or sweated through the night, the smell clings to your skin, hair, and fabric. A shower with soap and a full change of clothes can make a bigger difference than any mint. If you tend to sweat heavily after drinking, our guide to [night sweats after drinking](/never-hungover/night-sweats-after-drinking) explains why.

### 6. Use cover-ups strategically

Once you've done the steps above, mints, sugar-free gum, or a coffee can cover whatever is left from your mouth. Choose sugar-free options, since sugar feeds the bacteria that make breath worse later.

## What Doesn't Work (Despite What You've Heard)

A lot of advice online sounds clever but has no good evidence behind it.

- **Peanut butter, coffee beans, or lemon "to fool a breathalyzer."** These may cover the smell for a few minutes, but there is no good evidence that any food lowers a breathalyzer reading. The device measures alcohol from deep in your lungs, not the odor in your mouth.
- **Cold showers or exercise to sweat it out.** You lose only a tiny amount of alcohol through sweat. Working out while hungover can also leave you more dehydrated.
- **Coffee to sober up.** Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol. Feeling awake and being sober are not the same thing.
- **"Detox" drinks and charcoal.** There is no good evidence that activated charcoal pulls alcohol out of your body in any useful way, and detox drinks don't change how fast your liver works.
- **Holding your breath or breathing a certain way.** This changes how a breathalyzer sample is collected, not the alcohol in your blood.

## Why Do I Smell Like Alcohol the Next Day?

This is one of the most common versions of the question, and the answer is usually simple: you still have alcohol in your body, or you recently did.

If you drank heavily late into the night, your liver may still be working through it when you wake up. As a rough guide, if you had eight drinks and stopped at 2 a.m., it could easily take until mid-morning or later to clear them, and longer if you're smaller, drank on an empty stomach, or are a slower metabolizer. While that's happening, alcohol is still leaving through your lungs and skin.

Even after your blood alcohol reaches zero, a few things can keep the smell going:

- **Your skin, hair, and clothes** soaked up the smell overnight.
- **Your bedroom and bedding** hold the smell too. People often notice that a closed room smells boozy after a night out.
- **A dry mouth** from the night before makes everything smell stronger until saliva gets going again.
- **By-products** of alcohol breakdown can linger slightly longer than the alcohol itself.

The practical takeaway: if other people can smell alcohol on you the next morning, treat that as a sign that you may not be fully sober yet. That matters for driving, which we cover below. For a detailed timeline of how long the smell and breathalyzer readings last, see our guide to [how long alcohol stays on your breath](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-on-your-breath).

## Why Do I Smell Like Alcohol Through My Skin?

Many people notice the smell isn't only on their breath. It seems to come out of their pores. That isn't your imagination. A small share of the alcohol you drink leaves through your skin, either as vapor or in sweat. This is how transdermal alcohol monitors measure drinking without a breath or blood sample.

The skin smell tends to be strongest when:

- You drank a lot, so there's more alcohol to clear
- You slept warm or under heavy covers and sweated overnight
- You haven't showered yet

The fix is the same as above: time, then soap and water and clean clothes. Deodorant can help with general sweat odor, but it won't stop alcohol from leaving through your skin while it's still in your blood.

## Does the Type of Drink Change the Smell?

Somewhat, yes. Pure ethanol has a fairly mild smell. The stronger, more recognizable odors come from the other compounds in each drink.

| Drink | Why it can smell strong |
|---|---|
| Beer | Hops, malt, and yeast leave a distinctive, lingering odor in the mouth. |
| Red wine | Rich in congeners and tannins, and it can stain the tongue and teeth. |
| Whiskey, brandy, dark rum | Higher in congeners from aging in wood barrels. |
| Gin | Juniper and other botanicals give a sharp, recognizable smell. |
| Vodka | Fewer flavor compounds, so it's often said to smell less. But the lung part is the same, because that comes from the alcohol itself. |

The common belief that vodka "doesn't smell" is only half true. It may leave less flavor in your mouth, but the alcohol coming from your lungs smells the same no matter what you drank. The amount of alcohol matters much more than the type.

## Can You Get Rid of Alcohol Breath Fast?

Not completely. You can make the mouth part go away in about five minutes with a thorough brush, a tongue scrape, and a glass of water. You can make the skin part much better with a shower and fresh clothes. But the lung part lasts as long as alcohol remains in your blood, and no product or trick speeds that up enough to matter.

If you have a meeting, a family event, or a date in an hour, the realistic goal is "less noticeable," not "gone." Do the cleaning steps, eat something, drink water, and keep a little distance in close conversation.

## Alcohol Breath and Driving the Next Morning

This is where alcohol breath stops being a social problem and becomes a safety one.

If you can still smell alcohol on your own breath, or someone tells you that you smell of it, you may still be over the legal limit to drive. Many people are caught on the morning after, not the night before, because they slept for a few hours and assumed they were fine. Sleep doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. It just passes the time.

A few points worth knowing:

- **Mints and mouthwash don't change a breathalyzer reading in any useful way.** Police breath tests are designed to measure air from deep in the lungs, and officers typically wait a set period before testing so that alcohol in the mouth, including from mouthwash, has time to disappear.
- **Alcohol-based mouthwash can briefly raise a reading.** Using it right before a test can work against you, not for you.
- **Feeling fine is not a reliable test.** Your coordination and judgment can be affected even when you don't feel drunk.

To be completely clear: masking alcohol breath never makes it safe to drive. Mints, gum, and mouthwash change how you smell, not how much alcohol is in your blood or how impaired you are. If you're unsure, don't drive. Get a ride, take public transport, or wait. Our guide to [how long after drinking you can drive](/never-hungover/how-long-after-drinking-can-you-drive) gives more detail on timing, and our guide to [driving hungover](/never-hungover/driving-hungover) explains why the morning after can be risky even once your blood alcohol is back to zero.

## When a Strange Breath Smell Isn't About Alcohol

Sometimes people search for alcohol breath because they notice a boozy, sweet, or fruity smell they can't explain. Usually it's simply leftover alcohol. But some breath smells can be a sign of a medical problem, and a couple of them are serious.

- **Fruity or nail-polish-remover breath** can come from ketones, compounds your body makes when it burns fat instead of sugar. This can happen on a low-carb diet or after fasting. It can also happen with diabetic ketoacidosis, a dangerous complication of diabetes.
- **After a long stretch of heavy drinking with little food**, some people develop a condition called alcoholic ketoacidosis, which can also cause a fruity breath smell along with vomiting and stomach pain.
- **Breath that smells like alcohol when you haven't been drinking** has several possible causes, from ketosis to a rare condition in which gut yeast makes alcohol. Our guide to [breath that smells like alcohol without drinking](/never-hungover/breath-smells-like-alcohol-without-drinking) walks through each one.

> **When to see a doctor.** For most social drinkers, alcohol breath is harmless and fades within a day. **Get medical help promptly if** your breath smells fruity or like nail-polish remover and you also feel very thirsty, are peeing a lot, are vomiting, have stomach pain, are breathing fast, or feel confused or unusually weak. This is especially urgent if you have diabetes. Also see a doctor if your breath smells of alcohol when you haven't had any, or if you have constant bad breath that doesn't improve with good brushing and flossing. **Call 911** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't leave them to sleep it off. If you notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart whenever you go a day or two without drinking, tell a doctor. Stopping suddenly after a long stretch of heavy drinking can be dangerous, and a doctor can help you do it safely.

## How to Prevent Alcohol Breath Next Time

Since the smell mostly depends on how much alcohol is in your blood, the best prevention is simply drinking less, or drinking more slowly. A few habits help:

- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your blood, which keeps peak levels lower.
- **Alternate each drink with a glass of water.** This slows your pace and keeps your mouth from drying out.
- **Stop earlier in the evening.** The earlier you stop, the more time your liver has before morning.
- **Choose lower-strength drinks.** A light beer or a wine spritzer delivers less alcohol per glass than a strong cocktail.
- **Brush your teeth before bed.** It cuts down on the mouth layer of the smell the next day.
- **Keep water by the bed.** Sipping during the night helps with dry mouth.

Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers these and other habits with the best evidence behind them.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take around drinking. It's been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and on the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's promising, not proven.

To be clear about what it can't do: there is no good evidence that DHM gets rid of alcohol breath, lowers a breathalyzer reading, or makes you sober faster in any way that matters for driving. If you smell of alcohol the next morning, DHM won't change that, and it is never a reason to drive sooner.

Some people take it as part of a routine to feel better the morning after a night out. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Drinking less, eating, and hydrating will always do more for your breath than any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol breath mostly comes from your lungs, not your mouth, so mints and mouthwash can only cover part of it.
- Time is the only thing that clears the lung part. Your liver works at roughly one drink per hour, and nothing meaningfully speeds that up.
- What helps: brushing your teeth and tongue, drinking water, eating breakfast, and showering and changing clothes.
- Smelling of alcohol the next morning usually means alcohol is still in your system, so don't drive until you're sure it has cleared.
- A fruity or nail-polish smell with thirst, vomiting, or confusion, or a boozy smell when you haven't been drinking, is a reason to see a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do you get rid of alcohol breath fast?**

You can't remove it completely until your body has cleared the alcohol, because most of the smell comes from your lungs. You can make it much less noticeable in a few minutes: brush your teeth and tongue, floss, drink a large glass of water, eat something that needs chewing, and shower and change your clothes. Then use sugar-free gum or mints to cover what's left.

**Why do I smell like alcohol the next day?**

Usually because alcohol is still in your body. After a heavy night, your liver may still be clearing it well into the morning, and while that happens alcohol leaves through your breath and skin. Your clothes, hair, and bedding can also hold the smell, and a dry mouth makes it worse. If you smell strongly of alcohol the next day, assume you may not be fully sober and don't drive.

**Does mouthwash get rid of alcohol breath?**

Only partly. Mouthwash freshens your mouth and kills odor-causing bacteria, but it can't reach the alcohol coming from your lungs. Many mouthwashes also contain alcohol, which can make you smell more like alcohol for a short time and can briefly raise a breathalyzer reading. An alcohol-free mouthwash is the better choice.

**Can you get rid of alcohol breath to pass a breathalyzer?**

No. Breathalyzers measure alcohol from air deep in your lungs, which reflects the alcohol in your blood. There is no good evidence that mints, gum, peanut butter, coffee, or any other food or trick lowers the reading in a meaningful way. The only thing that lowers it is time. If you're unsure whether you're under the limit, don't drive.

**Why do I smell like alcohol through my skin?**

A small amount of the alcohol you drink leaves your body through your skin and sweat. That's how the alcohol-monitoring ankle bracelets some courts use work. The smell is strongest after heavy drinking and a sweaty night. A shower and clean clothes help a lot, but the smell from your skin continues until the alcohol is out of your blood.

**Does vodka leave less alcohol breath than beer or wine?**

It may leave less flavor in your mouth, because vodka has fewer of the extra compounds that give beer, wine, and dark spirits their strong smells. But the part of the smell that comes from your lungs is caused by the alcohol itself, so it's the same whatever you drank. How much alcohol you had matters far more than which drink it was.

**How long does alcohol breath last?**

It lasts roughly as long as alcohol stays in your blood, which depends on how much you drank, your size, whether you ate, and how quickly your liver works. The body clears about one standard drink per hour on average, so a heavy night can mean smelling of alcohol well into the next morning. The mouth part of the smell fades much faster, especially after brushing.

**When should I worry about breath that smells like alcohol?**

See a doctor if your breath smells of alcohol when you haven't been drinking, or if it smells fruity or like nail-polish remover along with strong thirst, frequent peeing, vomiting, stomach pain, fast breathing, or confusion. These can be signs of conditions like diabetic ketoacidosis that need prompt care. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking is hard to wake or breathing slowly.
